statement: In healthy volunteers scanned while racemic or (S)-ketamine was being infused, brain activity measured as glucose use or the fMRI signal goes up rather than down, and most at the front. In 10 volunteers given racemic ketamine, whole-brain glucose metabolism rose 24.5% (SD 14.3) from each person's own drug-free scan and rose in every participant (p<0.01); the rise was largest in the anterior cingulate (34%) and frontal cortex (30 to 34%) and smallest in the occipitomedial cortex (16 to 17%), with no decrease in absolute glucose metabolism in any region examined, although relative metabolism (each region divided by the whole brain) fell in the left temporomedial and occipitomedial cortex, and front-to-back ratios shifted accordingly (Vollenweider et al., 1997b). In a second group of 10 given the (S)-form, regional increases ran from 19.6% in the frontomedial to 27.35% in the parietal cortex, with cortical regions about 2 to 3 times more affected than deeper structures and the whole-brain change (12%) not reaching significance (Vollenweider et al., 1997a). A 2024 meta-analysis that pooled the published peak coordinates of 33 functional-imaging studies in 628 healthy volunteers, and whose confidence the editors rate critically low, found only two clusters that survived correction for multiple testing, each resting on part of the 395 people in the two analyses that produced results rather than on all 628: more activity at rest in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (658 voxels, 495 after correction) and, during executive-function tasks, in the right Heschl's gyrus (160 voxels, 142 after correction); across all 23 task studies together nothing was significant in either direction, and no decrease is reported in any of the three analyses, which the review states outright for the pooled task analysis and which is what its table shows for the other two (Ait Bentaleb et al., 2024). Two things sit beside this. In the same Zurich laboratory the equimolar (R)-form moved the other way, lowering glucose metabolism significantly in two regions (Vollenweider et al., 1997a; the figures are on card sc_vollenweider_1997a), so the direction given here is that of racemic and (S)-ketamine. And the 2016 review reports, second-hand, that at an anaesthetic amount of (S)-ketamine whole-brain blood flow rose while the metabolic rate of oxygen and of glucose stayed virtually unchanged, so blood flow and energy use need not move together. What these scans cannot show is which change produces which experience: both 1997 studies report every symptom-to-brain correlation as a significance level with a direction and print no correlation coefficient anywhere, they made about 150 to 180 comparisons without correcting for their number, which the enantiomer paper states and calls exploratory while the companion paper calls its correlational results only preliminary and nowhere says whether any correction was made; one of them had no dummy condition and in the other every participant recognised the drug. All of this describes a single session with ketamine in the body, not any lasting change. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: When people are given ketamine in a scanner, their brain uses more energy, not less, especially at the front. In one study of 10 healthy people, whole-brain energy use rose by about a quarter, and it rose in every single person. A 2024 summary of 33 imaging studies found the clearest agreement in one spot near the front of the brain at rest. One mirror-image form of ketamine, called R, moved the other way and lowered energy use in two areas. These scans cannot show which brain change causes which feeling, and they only describe what happens while the drug is in the body.
population: Healthy volunteers screened to be free of psychiatric history and of non-medical drug use: 10 in each of the two Zurich PET studies (6 men and 4 women in each), and 628 people in the 33 studies pooled by the 2024 meta-analysis, of whom 395 are in the two analyses that produced results
exposure: Subanaesthetic intravenous ketamine during the scan (study conditions in Zurich: a 20 mg or 15 mg induction amount in saline over 5 minutes, 5 minutes with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.02–0.03 or 0.014–0.02 mg/kg/min for 60 or 53 minutes; in the pooled studies, intravenous amounts the review describes as within the range used in depression trials)
comparator: The same people's drug-free baseline scan (1997b) or placebo scan (1997a); placebo or a baseline condition in the pooled studies, 7 of 10 resting-state studies being within-person
outcome: Whole-brain and regional glucose metabolism, cerebral blood flow or activation during the drug
magnitude: Vollenweider et al. (1997b), racemic, n=10: whole-brain glucose metabolism +24.5% (SD 14.3, Wilcoxon p<0.01, higher in every participant); cingulate anterior +34%, frontal +30 to 34%, insula +19 to 23%, parietal +18 to 25%, somatosensory +19 to 25%, motor +15 to 18%, temporal +16 to 19%, occipitomedial +16 to 17%; no decreases. Frontomedial/temporomedial ratio 1.31→1.44 (left) and 1.41→1.53 (right), frontomedial/occipitomedial 1.04→1.14 and 1.06→1.16 (all p<0.05). Vollenweider et al. (1997a), (S)-ketamine, n=10: frontomedial +19.6%, frontolateral +20.1%, cingulate anterior +23.5%, cingulate posterior +24.0%, parietal +27.35%; thalamus +17% (p<0.07); whole brain +12% (p<0.09, not significant). Ait Bentaleb et al. (2024): resting state, left anterior cingulate/paracingulate BA 24 (MNI 0; 30; 20), Z=4.265, p<0.001, 658 voxels, 495 after correction; uncorrected only, right insula BA 47 (36; 24; −6), Z=3.432, 30 voxels, and right fusiform gyrus BA 30 (22; −34; −16), Z=2.933, 26 voxels. Executive-function tasks (9 studies): right Heschl's gyrus BA 48 (44; −16; 6), Z=3.306, 160 voxels, 142 after correction; uncorrected right rostral anterior cingulate BA 10 (6; 52; 8), Z=2.889, 26 voxels. No effect size or interval is recoverable from a coordinate-based meta-analysis.

evidence.locator: Results › Absolute whole brain and regional cerebral metabolic rates (3.2), 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: Whole-brain glucose metabolism rose in all 10 participants, by 24.5% (SD 14.3) from baseline to the ketamine scan (Wilcoxon p<0.01). The increase was largest in the cingulate anterior (34%) and frontal cortex (30 to 34%) and smaller in the insula (19 to 23%), parietal (18 to 25%), somatosensory (19 to 25%), motor (15 to 18%) and temporal (16 to 19%) cortex, with the smallest increase in the occipitomedial cortex (16 to 17%); no decreases in glucose metabolism were found in any region examined.

evidence.locator: Table 2, columns Baseline and Ketamine with their P-levels
evidence.extracted: Ratios between regions shifted towards the front: frontomedial/temporomedial 1.31 (SD 0.08) to 1.44 (0.12) on the left and 1.41 (0.10) to 1.53 (0.17) on the right; frontomedial/occipitomedial 1.04 to 1.14 and 1.06 to 1.16 (all p<0.05); frontolateral/temporomedial 1.30 to 1.47 (p<0.01) and 1.31 to 1.46 (p<0.05); frontolateral/putamen 1.00 to 1.09 and 0.98 to 1.09 (p<0.01). More ratios changed, and more changed at p<0.01, on the left than on the right.

evidence.locator: Results › Relative metabolic rates and metabolic ratios (3.3), 1st paragraph; Results › Plasma ketamine levels (3.1)
evidence.extracted: Once each region was divided by the whole-brain value, the picture is a redistribution rather than a uniform rise: relative values rose in the frontolateral cortex on both sides and in the left anterior cingulate and fell in the left temporomedial and occipitomedial cortex (p<0.05), with the same direction at trend level on the right (p<0.06). Blood levels during the scans ranged from 240 to 1145 ng/mL (mean 557, SD 254) and the first psychotic symptoms came on average 4.5 minutes after the start, at a mean level of 386 ng/mL; blood levels did not correlate significantly with the metabolic changes.

The study was open: 15 volunteers were told they would receive a baseline scan and two further scans with a stimulant or a hallucinogenic drug, and the comparison for the drug scan is a drug-free baseline scan, not a dummy infusion. Each person received two of the three drugs, so the ketamine results come from 10 of the 15.

evidence.locator: Results › Absolute and relative cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (3.3), 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: With (S)-ketamine in a different group of 10 volunteers, glucose metabolism rose in the frontomedial (19.6%), frontolateral (20.1%), cingulate anterior (23.5%), cingulate posterior (24.0%) and parietal (27.35%) cortex on both sides, and in the somatosensory (21.1%) and motor (23.0%) cortex on the left only; the thalamus was the only subcortical region with a bilateral increase and only at trend level (17%, p<0.07), and whole-brain metabolism rose 12% without reaching significance (p<0.09). Relative values rose in the frontomedial (7.7%), frontolateral (8.4%) and posterior cingulate (12.5%) cortex and the left parietal cortex (18.2%) and fell in the left temporomedial cortex (4.8%).

The authors state that no correction was made for the number of comparisons and that the results should therefore be read as exploratory; the editors' tally of the comparisons displayed or reported in this paper is about 180, and about 150 in the companion paper.

evidence.locator: Table 2, column r(sp) (p. 33); Results, 1st paragraph on p. 34
evidence.extracted: The column headed as Spearman correlations in fact holds significance levels carrying the sign of the correlation: the values printed as −0.02 and −0.001 for the frontolateral-putamen ratio against the hallucinatory-disintegration syndrome are given in the text as p<0.02 (left) and p<0.001 (right). No correlation coefficient is printed anywhere, so the size of any symptom-to-metabolism association in these studies is unknown and cannot be used in a claim.

evidence.locator: Table 3, resting-state and executive-functions rows with the footnote
evidence.extracted: Pooled peak coordinates, ketamine against placebo or baseline. At rest: left anterior cingulate and paracingulate gyri, BA 24 (MNI 0; 30; 20), Z = 4.265, p < 0.001, 658 voxels, the only cluster to survive correction for multiple testing (495 voxels in the footnote); right insula, BA 47 (36; 24; −6), Z = 3.432, 30 voxels, and right fusiform gyrus, BA 30 (22; −34; −16), Z = 2.933, p < 0.002, 26 voxels, both at the uncorrected threshold only. During executive-function tasks: right Heschl's gyrus, BA 48 (44; −16; 6), Z = 3.306, 160 voxels, surviving correction with 142 voxels, and right anterior cingulate, BA 10 (6; 52; 8), Z = 2.889, 26 voxels, uncorrected only. Every result is an increase in activation.

evidence.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Results › Meta-analysis of task-related activity, 1st paragraph; Results › Heterogeneity and publication bias
evidence.extracted: 33 articles were retained, 10 resting-state (198 participants, 75% male, mean age 27.71 years) and 23 task-activation studies (371 participants, 72% male, mean age 27.4). Across all 23 task studies taken together, no cluster of increased or decreased activation reached significance; the executive-function finding comes from the 9 studies of that domain. Heterogeneity was between 0.15% and 6.45% and Egger's tests gave all p-values above 0.24, which with 9 or 10 studies carries almost no information.

The authors name the small evidence base as their first limitation: 628 participants in all and 395 in the two analyses that produced results, too few studies to detect moderators or to analyse other cognitive domains. Of the 19 studies in those two analyses only 8 reported a blood ketamine level, mean 98.08 ng/mL, range 16.6 to 183; no included study gave ketamine over a prolonged period, so nothing here speaks to repeated use.

evidence.locator: Section 6.3.2 Effects on Neurotoxicity, Neuroprotection, and Intracranial Pressure, 5th paragraph (begins p. 11)
evidence.extracted: The review reports, second-hand from a PET study in healthy volunteers, that an anaesthetic amount of S-ketamine increased whole-brain cerebral blood flow by 36% and a subanaesthetic amount by 13%, while the metabolic rate of oxygen and glucose remained virtually unaffected, so that perfusion rose most in the insula and anterior cingulate; it adds that a similar study with low-dose racemic ketamine showed a tendency for glucose metabolism and blood flow to rise with the amount given.

risk_of_bias.note: The racemic study was open with a drug-free baseline instead of a dummy infusion, and in the enantiomer study every participant recognised the drug, so expectancy is uncontrolled for both the scans and the ratings; regions of interest were placed by hand with no stated blinding; about 150 to 180 comparisons were made without correction and regions, ratios and correlations are reported selectively (cards sc_vollenweider_1997a and sc_vollenweider_1997b, both high). The 2024 meta-analysis appraised none of its primary studies, has no protocol and is rated critically low confidence (card sc_ait_bentaleb_2024).

inconsistency.note: The direction is the same everywhere: increases, largest frontally, and no decrease in any analysis. The meta-analysis's null result across all task domains is explained by pooling studies of different cognitive tasks.

indirectness.note: Healthy volunteers scanned during the drug, which is what the claim states. Nothing here speaks to repeated use, to people who use ketamine outside a laboratory or to people with a psychiatric diagnosis.

imprecision.note: Ten people in each Zurich study and 5 to 34 per pooled study; a coordinate-based meta-analysis recovers no effect size or interval, and the two corrected clusters are the only results that survive a stringent threshold.

publication_bias.note: Egger's tests were run and were null, but with 9 or 10 studies they have almost no power, and only studies that published whole-brain peaks can enter such a meta-analysis.

dose_response.note: Blood level did not predict the metabolic change in the racemic study, and every dose moderator in the meta-analysis was null in 9 or 10 studies.

grade.reasoning: Within-person challenge studies start high (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −2: one study had no dummy condition at all, the other's blind did not hold, and both report many uncorrected comparisons selectively, while the meta-analysis pooling the wider literature appraised no primary study. Imprecision −1: ten people per Zurich study, small primary studies, and no recoverable effect size from the pooled maps. Not downgraded for inconsistency or indirectness. Very low, the floor. Replicated in direction, but counted carefully: the two FDG studies come from one laboratory in Zurich and share their method, so the independent support is the 2024 meta-analysis, whose resting-state cluster sits in the same anterior cingulate region and which does not include either Zurich study.
